sections.title: 1.4 True north and how to measure from it

chapters.html:
Navigation starts with three questions: what shape is the Earth, how do we say where a point is on it, and how do we say which way we are pointing. This chapter answers all three. It builds the grid of latitude and longitude, the units that come from it, and the three norths (true, magnetic and compass) that every heading and track is measured from. The chapters that follow on speed, charts and great circles all use these ideas.

1.1 The shape of the Earth

The Earth is not a perfect sphere. If the oceans were free to settle under gravity alone and could flow through channels under the continents, mean sea level would form a surface called the geoid. It is an equipotential surface of gravity, shaped only by gravity and the centrifugal force of the Earth's rotation. Because mass is unevenly spread inside the Earth, the geoid is irregular, with bumps and hollows of up to about ±100 m. Elevations and altitudes above mean sea level are measured from the geoid. 01.01.01.01

An irregular surface is no use for drawing a grid, so mapmakers replace it with a smooth mathematical shape, an ellipsoid. The Earth is close to an oblate ellipsoid: flattened at the poles and bulging at the equator, with a polar diameter about 43 km shorter than the equatorial one (a flattening of about 1/298). Many ellipsoids have been used for national mapping, each fitted to its own region. For aviation ICAO requires all published coordinates to be on WGS-84 (World Geodetic System 1984), the global ellipsoid also used by GPS. Mixing coordinates from different datums can shift a position by hundreds of metres, which matters for RNAV approaches and database coding. GNSS heights are measured above the ellipsoid; the difference from height above MSL is the geoid undulation. 01.01.01.02

Exam trap. The geoid is the irregular one; the ellipsoid is the smooth model. The geoid is shaped by gravity and centrifugal force only, not by tides or wind.

The size of the Earth comes straight from the definition of the nautical mile. A circle has 360° × 60' = 21 600 minutes of arc, and one minute of latitude is about one nautical mile, so the circumference is about 21 600 NM, or about 40 000 km. Pole to pole is half of that, 10 800 NM, and the equator to a pole is 90 × 60 = 5400 NM. 01.01.01.03

Key numbers · the Earth

Quantity Value
Circumference ≈ 21 600 NM ≈ 40 000 km
Equator to pole 5400 NM
1° of latitude 60 NM, anywhere
Flattening ≈ 1/298 (polar diameter ≈ 43 km shorter)
Reference ellipsoid WGS-84 (ICAO Annex 15)

1.2 Rotation, seasons and daylight

The Earth spins on its axis from west to east, anticlockwise seen from above the North Pole. Relative to the Sun one turn takes 24 hours, so the Sun appears to move westward at 15° of longitude per hour. The Earth orbits the Sun once in about 365¼ days, in a plane called the ecliptic. Its spin axis is tilted 23½° from the perpendicular to the ecliptic, which is the same as 66½° to the plane of the ecliptic, and the axis keeps pointing the same way in space all year. The orbit is slightly elliptical, and the Earth is in fact closest to the Sun in early January, during the northern winter. 01.01.02.01

Because of the tilt, the latitude where the Sun is overhead at noon, its declination, moves through the year between 23½° N at the June solstice (about 21 June) and 23½° S at the December solstice (about 21 December). It crosses the equator at the equinoxes, about 20 March and 23 September. When the Sun is high, each square metre of ground receives more energy (more insolation) and the day is longer. At the equinoxes day and night are about 12 hours everywhere. Beyond the polar circles at 66½° there is at least one day of continuous daylight in summer and of continuous night in winter. At the equator the day is about 12 hours all year, and the yearly variation grows with latitude. 01.01.02.02

Exam trap. The seasons come from the tilt of the axis, not from the distance to the Sun. Both 23½° and 66½° appear in questions: one is measured from the perpendicular, the other from the plane.

1.3 Latitude and longitude

A position is given by geodetic latitude and longitude on the WGS-84 ellipsoid. Geodetic latitude is the angle between the normal to the ellipsoid at the point and the plane of the equator. It is not the angle at the Earth's centre, which is the geocentric latitude and differs slightly because the Earth is flattened. Charts and GNSS use geodetic latitude. Coordinates are written latitude first, for example N40°25.5' W003°41.2'. 01.02.01.01

Latitude is the angular distance north or south of the equator, from 0° to 90° N or S. Parallels of latitude are circles parallel to the equator joining points of equal latitude. The equator is the only parallel that is a great circle; all the others are small circles, and they get shorter towards the poles: the length of a parallel is the length of the equator × cos latitude. At 60° a parallel is half as long as the equator. 01.02.01.02

The difference of latitude (d.lat) is the arc of a meridian between two parallels. If both points are in the same hemisphere, subtract their latitudes; if they are in opposite hemispheres, add them. Name the result N or S by the direction of travel. Because one minute of latitude is one nautical mile, d.lat in minutes is the distance in NM along a meridian. 01.02.01.03

Worked example · d.lat. From 52°30' N to 47°10' N: same hemisphere, subtract: d.lat = 5°20' S = 320', so 320 NM along the meridian. From 10° N to 15° S: opposite hemispheres, add: d.lat = 25° S.

Longitude is the angle east or west of the prime meridian through Greenwich, from 0° to 180° E or W. Meridians are semi-great circles running from pole to pole. A meridian together with its anti-meridian, 180° away, forms a complete great circle. All meridians meet at the poles and are parallel to each other only where they cross the equator. 180° E and 180° W are the same meridian, which is the basis of the date line (Chapter 6). 01.02.01.04

The difference of longitude (d.long) is the smaller angle at the pole between two meridians. In the same hemisphere, subtract; in opposite hemispheres, add, and if the sum exceeds 180°, take it from 360° and reverse the direction, because the shorter way is then across the 180° meridian. 01.02.01.05

Worked example · d.long across the date line. From 170° E to 160° W: 170 + 160 = 330°, more than 180°. So d.long = 360 − 330 = 30° E, travelling east across the 180° meridian.

Exam trap. d.long is an angle, not a distance. It becomes a distance only when multiplied by cos latitude (departure, Chapter 2).

1.4 True north and how to measure from it

True north (TN) is the direction along a meridian towards the geographic North Pole. True directions are measured clockwise from TN, from 000° to 360°. Charts are drawn relative to true north, so a track measured on a chart with a protractor is a true track. Some directions you meet in flight are true and others magnetic: winds in METARs, TAFs and wind charts are true, while the wind given by ATIS or the tower for landing, runway directions, VOR radials and most AIP en-route tracks are magnetic. 01.03.01.01

To measure a true direction on a chart, align the protractor with a meridian (never with the edge of the chart) and measure clockwise from it at the point you are interested in. On a Mercator chart all meridians are parallel, so a straight line crosses them all at the same angle. On a Lambert or polar chart the meridians converge, so a straight line crosses each one at a different angle. Measuring at the mid-meridian gives approximately the rhumb-line track; measuring at the departure meridian gives the initial great-circle track (Chapter 4). 01.03.01.02

1.5 Magnetic north and variation

Magnetic north (MN) is the direction a freely suspended magnet points: along the horizontal part of the Earth's magnetic field towards the north magnetic pole. That pole is not at the geographic pole. It lies in the Arctic Ocean north of Canada and is drifting towards Siberia. Close to the magnetic poles the field points steeply downwards (large dip), the horizontal part is weak and the compass becomes unreliable. 01.03.01.03

Variation is the angle between true north and magnetic north at a place. It is named East if magnetic north lies east of true north, and West if it lies west. To convert: True = Magnetic + East variation, and True = Magnetic − West variation. The memory aid is "variation east, magnetic least; variation west, magnetic best". Lines joining places of equal variation are isogonals; the line of zero variation is the agonic line. 01.03.01.04

Worked example · variation. True track 090°, variation 5° W. Magnetic is "best" with west variation, so MT = 090 + 5 = 095°.

Variation changes with position, shown by the isogonals on a chart, and with time. As the magnetic poles drift, variation everywhere changes slowly; this secular change is a few minutes of arc per year in Europe. Charts give the variation for a stated year and the annual change, so add the annual change × the number of years since then. There are also small daily changes, and sudden disturbances during magnetic storms caused by solar activity, which also upset HF radio. Because of secular change, runway designators and VOR alignments are updated from time to time. 01.03.01.05

Exam trap. Isogonal = equal variation; agonic = zero variation; isoclinal = equal dip; aclinic = zero dip. A VOR radial uses the variation at the station.

1.6 Compass north and deviation

Compass north (CN) is where the aircraft's own compass actually points. It differs from magnetic north because the aircraft has magnetic fields of its own, from ferrous parts and electrical currents. Unlike magnetic north, compass north depends on the aircraft and on its heading. 01.03.01.06

Deviation is the angle between magnetic north and compass north, named East (+) if compass north lies east of magnetic north and West (−) if west. Magnetic = Compass + East deviation; Magnetic = Compass − West deviation. Deviation changes with the aircraft's heading and with electrical load, so it is measured in a compass swing and listed on a deviation card for each heading. Swing the compass again after major modifications or avionics changes, after a lightning strike, and after moving to a base at a very different magnetic latitude. 01.03.01.07

The two corrections chain together from the compass to true: C → D → M → V → T (Compass, Deviation, Magnetic, Variation, True), adding East and subtracting West at each step. Going the other way, from true to compass, reverse the signs.

Worked example · C–D–M–V–T. Compass heading 270°, deviation 2° E, variation 4° W. Magnetic heading = 270 + 2 = 272°. True heading = 272 − 4 = 268°.

Exam trap. Deviation depends on the aircraft's heading; variation depends on the aircraft's position. Never apply variation to a drift angle: drift is an angle between two directions, not a direction.

1.7 Heading, track and drift

The heading is where the nose points; the track is the path over the ground. The wind makes them differ. Drift is the angle between the heading and the track made good: the aircraft is blown downwind, and drift is named right (starboard) or left (port). The wind correction angle (WCA) is the angle between the track you want and the heading you must fly to make it good; it is applied into the wind. In a steady wind the WCA has the same size as the drift it cancels. With the wind from the left, the drift is to the right, so the heading must be to the left of the track. 01.03.02.02

So track made good = heading + right drift, or heading − left drift. Use true heading with true track, magnetic with magnetic. 01.03.02.03

Worked example · track from heading. Heading 075° T, drift 7° left. Track = 075 − 7 = 068° T.

How big is the drift? It depends on the crosswind component (XWC), the part of the wind blowing across the track: XWC = wind speed × sin(wind angle), where the wind angle is between the wind direction and the track or runway. For mental dead reckoning (MDR), use the clock code: treat the angle as minutes of an hour, so 10° ≈ 1/6 of the wind, 20° ≈ 1/3, 30° ≈ 1/2, 40° ≈ 2/3, 50° ≈ 5/6, and 60° or more ≈ the full wind. Use the same reference for both directions: true wind with true track, magnetic wind with a runway. 01.03.02.01

Worked example · crosswind. Track 090°, W/V 130/30. Angle 40° → XWC ≈ 2/3 × 30 = 20 kt from the right (exactly 30 × sin 40° = 19.3 kt). The clock code slightly overestimates around 40–50°.

The track error (TKE) is the angle between the required track and the track actually made good, named by which side of the planned track the aircraft has gone. It appears whenever the WCA you flew does not match the real drift: a wrong forecast wind, or a heading flown carelessly. 01.03.02.04

Worked example · track error. Required track 100°. You fly heading 094° (WCA 6° left), but the actual drift is only 2° right. Track made good = 094 + 2 = 096°. TKE = 4° left.

1.8 Off-track corrections: the 1 in 60 rule

The 1 in 60 rule says that 1° of angle corresponds to 1 NM of offset for every 60 NM of distance. It is accurate enough for angles up to about 20° and lets you correct a track error in your head. At a fix that shows you off track:

  • Track error (TE) = off-track distance × 60 / distance flown.
  • Closing angle (CA) = off-track distance × 60 / distance to go.
  • To fly direct to the next waypoint, alter heading by TE + CA towards the track.
  • To regain the track in the same distance as already flown, alter by 2 × TE, then turn back by TE once on track.

01.03.02.05

Worked example · 1 in 60. After 40 NM you are 4 NM right of track, with 60 NM to go. TE = 4 × 60 / 40 = 6°; CA = 4 × 60 / 60 = 4°. Turn 10° left to reach the waypoint.

A fix also tells you the actual drift. If you know the heading you flew, the track made good from the last fix gives the drift: drift = track made good − heading, and the track made good is the required track corrected by TE. If you were already applying a WCA, the actual drift is not simply the TE. The new heading must allow for the actual drift as well as the closing angle. 01.03.02.06

Worked example · average drift. Heading 090° with no WCA. After 30 NM the fix is 3 NM left of the 090° track: TE = 3 × 60 / 30 = 6° left, so track made good = 084° and the average drift is 6° left.

Exam trap. Distance flown goes with the track error; distance to go goes with the closing angle. Swapping them is the classic mistake.

Check yourself

  1. Which forces shape the geoid, and what is WGS-84? Gravity and the centrifugal force of rotation only. WGS-84 is the reference ellipsoid ICAO requires for aeronautical coordinates.
  2. How long is 1° of latitude, and how far is it from the equator to a pole? 60 NM; 5400 NM.
  3. Find d.long from 175° W to 165° E. Opposite hemispheres: 175 + 165 = 340°, more than 180°, so d.long = 20° W.
  4. Compass heading 140°, deviation 3° W, variation 6° E. What is the true heading? Magnetic 137°, true 143°.
  5. Track 330°, W/V 300/40. What crosswind component, and which way is the drift? Angle 30°, so about 20 kt from the left; drift is to the right.
  6. After 45 NM you are 3 NM left of track with 75 NM to go. What heading change takes you direct to the waypoint? TE 4°, CA 2.4°, so about 6° right.
  7. Why is the Sun's declination never more than 23½°? Because the spin axis is tilted 23½° from the perpendicular to the ecliptic.

chapters.html:
With a grid and a north in place, navigation becomes arithmetic: how far, how fast, and therefore where and when. This chapter covers the units of distance, distances along the grid, airspeeds and Mach number, wind components and ground speed, the triangle of velocities, dead reckoning, and the rules of thumb for climbs and descents. Almost every calculation question in the exam is built from these pieces.

2.1 The nautical mile

The international nautical mile is exactly 1852 m. It is the average length of one minute of latitude on the WGS-84 ellipsoid. Because the ellipsoid is flatter near the poles, a minute of latitude there is slightly longer (about 1861 m) than at the equator (about 1843 m), but for navigation 1' of latitude = 1 NM, and 1° of latitude = 60 NM anywhere. 01.04.01.01

At the equator, which is a great circle, 1' of longitude is also about 1 NM. Away from the equator the meridians close in, and one minute of longitude covers only cos latitude NM: about 0.5 NM at 60°, and nothing at the poles. Never treat minutes of d.long as nautical miles except on the equator. 01.04.01.02

2.2 Units of distance

You need to move between five units without hesitation. 01.04.02.01

Key numbers · distance units

Unit Equals
1 NM 1852 m = 6076 ft ≈ 1.15 SM
1 SM (statute mile) 1609 m = 5280 ft
1 km 0.54 NM
1 m 3.28 ft
1 ft 0.3048 m = 12 in
1 in 2.54 cm

Worked example · conversions. 250 km = 250 / 1.852 = 135 NM. 3000 m = 3000 × 3.28 = 9843 ft.

Exam trap. km → NM: divide by 1.852 (or multiply by 0.54). NM → SM: multiply by 1.15. METAR visibility and RVR are in metres, cloud bases in feet.

2.3 Distances on the graticule

Three kinds of graticule distance appear in the exam. 01.04.03.01

  • Along a meridian, distance in NM = d.lat in minutes.
  • Across a pole, between points on opposite (antipodal) meridians, where d.long = 180°, the great-circle route goes over the pole. Distance = (90° − lat A) + (90° − lat B), in degrees × 60.
  • Along a parallel, the rhumb line east–west, the distance is the departure: departure (NM) = d.long (minutes) × cos latitude.

Working backwards gives a new position: d.lat (') = NM north or south; d.long (') = NM east or west ÷ cos latitude. If the route changes latitude, use the mean latitude.

Worked example · departure. Fly 600 NM east along 60° N. d.long = 600 / cos 60° = 600 / 0.5 = 1200' = 20°.

Worked example · across the pole. From 70° N 010° E to 75° N 170° W. d.long = 180°, so the great circle crosses the pole: (90 − 70) + (90 − 75) = 35° = 2100 NM. Along the parallel the same journey would be far longer, which is why polar routes exist.

2.4 Air distance and ground distance

Distance measured through the moving air mass is air distance, in nautical air miles (NAM). With a headwind the aircraft must fly more air miles to cover a given ground distance; with a tailwind, fewer. Flying higher raises the TAS for the same IAS and usually improves the specific range, but the ratio of air to ground distance depends only on TAS and ground speed. Range and fuel tables in aircraft manuals are often in NAM, so they must be converted with the wind. 01.04.04.01

Time is the same in both frames: t = NM / GS = NAM / TAS. Therefore NAM = NM × TAS / GS, and NM = NAM × GS / TAS. 01.04.04.02

Worked example · NAM. 500 NM over the ground, TAS 450 kt, 50 kt headwind so GS 400 kt. NAM = 500 × 450 / 400 = 562.5 NAM. A headwind must always give the larger number.

2.5 True airspeed and Mach number

The airspeed indicator measures dynamic pressure, so it reads correctly only at sea-level density. Corrected for instrument and position errors it gives the calibrated airspeed (CAS). The true airspeed (TAS), the actual speed through the air, is CAS corrected for density, that is for pressure altitude and temperature. On a mechanical computer (CRP or E6B), set the outside air temperature against the pressure altitude in the airspeed window, then read TAS on the outer scale opposite CAS on the inner scale. The rule of thumb is TAS ≈ CAS + 2 % per 1000 ft in ISA conditions. Above about FL 250 or M 0.5, compressibility makes the rule and the simple computer setting less accurate, and a compressibility correction or the Mach number is used. 01.05.01.01

Worked example · TAS rule of thumb. CAS 150 kt at FL 100: 10 × 2 % = 20 %, so TAS ≈ 150 × 1.20 = 180 kt. If the air is warmer than ISA, the TAS is a little higher.

The Mach number is TAS divided by the local speed of sound (LSS). The speed of sound depends only on temperature: LSS = 38.95 × √T kt, with T in kelvin. In ISA at sea level (288 K) LSS ≈ 661 kt; at the tropopause (−56.5 °C, 216.5 K) LSS ≈ 573 kt. So TAS = M × LSS, and the same TAS gives a higher Mach number in colder air. 01.05.02.01

Worked example · TAS from Mach. M 0.80 at −50 °C: T = 223 K, LSS = 38.95 × √223 ≈ 582 kt, TAS = 0.80 × 582 ≈ 466 kt.

How the three speeds move in a climb or descent follows from these two relationships. 01.05.03.01

  • Climbing at constant CAS: density falls, so TAS rises. Temperature falls too, so the speed of sound falls and the Mach number rises even faster than TAS.
  • Climbing at constant Mach below the tropopause: the temperature, and so the LSS, falls, so TAS falls; CAS falls too.
  • Constant Mach above the tropopause, in isothermal air: LSS is constant, so TAS is constant, while CAS keeps falling.

Jets therefore climb at a constant CAS and change to a constant Mach number at the crossover altitude, so that they do not run into the Mach limit (MMO). In the descent the order is reversed: constant Mach first, then constant CAS, and as CAS rises in the descent at constant Mach, the pilot watches VMO below the crossover.

2.6 Wind components and ground speed

The part of the wind along the track is the headwind or tailwind component: HWC or TWC = wind speed × cos(wind angle). Quick values: cos 30° ≈ 0.9, cos 45° ≈ 0.7, cos 60° = 0.5. A wind less than 90° from the nose is a headwind, more than 90° a tailwind; at 60° the headwind is only half the wind, at 90° nothing. 01.05.04.01

Worked example · components. Track 360°, W/V 030/40. Angle 30°: HWC = 40 × 0.87 ≈ 35 kt, XWC = 40 × 0.5 = 20 kt.

For small drift angles, GS ≈ TAS − HWC or TAS + TWC, and in reverse TAS ≈ GS + HWC. Ground speed is used for time and fuel; TAS for air distance. 01.05.04.02

There is a catch with strong crosswinds. When the aircraft crabs into wind, only TAS × cos WCA acts along the track; this is the effective TAS. With a pure crosswind, GS = TAS × cos WCA, which is less than TAS. At a WCA of 20°, cos 20° = 0.94, a 6 % loss. A 90° crosswind therefore still reduces the ground speed, which matters most for slow aircraft in strong winds. 01.05.04.03

2.7 The triangle of velocities

The triangle of velocities (TOV) adds two vectors to give a third. The air vector is true heading and TAS, drawn with one arrowhead. The wind vector is the wind velocity, drawn downwind with three arrowheads (a wind from 270° is drawn pointing east). The ground vector, track and GS with two arrowheads, closes the triangle from the start of the air vector to the end of the wind vector. Air vector + wind vector = ground vector, and the angle between the air and ground vectors is the drift. Any two complete vectors define the third. 01.06.01.01

There are three standard problems. 01.06.02.01

  1. Heading and GS (pre-flight planning), from track, TAS and W/V. On the computer: mark the wind down from the centre, set the track at the index, slide TAS under the centre, read the WCA and GS. By MDR: WCA = XWC / SF and GS ≈ TAS − HWC.
  2. The W/V (in flight), from heading, TAS, track and GS. On the computer: set the heading, TAS at the centre, mark the track and GS point, then rotate to read the wind.
  3. Track and GS (dead reckoning), from heading, TAS and W/V. On the computer: set the heading, mark the wind, read drift and GS; track = heading ± drift.

Problem 1 starts from the track and problem 3 from the heading. Mixing them up gives a drift error of up to twice the WCA. Check the answer: the heading must point into wind, and a headwind must lower the ground speed.

On the computer, the GS solution works the same way: wind direction under the index, wind speed marked up from the centre, track set, TAS under the centre, read drift and GS under the wind mark. By MDR, find the XWC with the clock code, WCA = XWC / SF with SF = TAS / 60, and GS = TAS × cos WCA − HWC. 01.05.04.04

Worked example · MDR ground speed. TAS 180 kt (SF 3), track 090°, W/V 060/30. Angle 30°: XWC ≈ 15 kt, so WCA = 15 / 3 = 5° left; HWC ≈ 26 kt, so GS ≈ 180 − 26 ≈ 154 kt.

2.8 Ground speed, distance and time

Distance = GS × time, so time = distance / GS and GS = distance / time. Working in minutes: time (min) = distance × 60 / GS. Take care converting decimals of an hour: 1.4 h is 1 h 24 min, not 1 h 40 min. 01.05.04.05

Worked example · time. 175 NM at GS 210 kt: 175 × 60 / 210 = 50 min.

To arrive at a waypoint at a set time, the required GS = distance to go / time available; then find the TAS needed from the wind component, and check it is within the speed range and the fuel plan. This is the basis of time-controlled arrivals. 01.05.04.06

Worked example · revised GS. 120 NM to go, and the waypoint must be reached in 25 min: GS = 120 × 60 / 25 = 288 kt.

Two fixes give the average GS: the distance between them divided by the time between them. Use the measured distance between the fixes, not the planned leg length. With the heading and TAS, the average GS and track also give the actual wind. 01.05.04.07

Worked example · average GS. Fixes 42 NM apart at 1012 and 1024 UTC (12 min): GS = 42 × 60 / 12 = 210 kt.

In flight the flight log is kept up to date. At each waypoint record the actual time of arrival (ATA), work out the actual GS and wind, revise the ETAs of the following legs (ATA + leg time at the new GS), and compare the fuel remaining with the plan. Time gained or lost × fuel flow = fuel gained or lost. Update the expected landing fuel and compare it with final reserve plus alternate fuel. The trend of the fuel deviation tells you more than a single reading. 01.05.05.01

2.9 Gradients and rates of climb and descent

Taking 1 NM ≈ 6000 ft turns gradients into simple rules based on the 1 in 60 rule:

  • gradient (°) ≈ (height difference (ft) / 100) / distance (NM)
  • gradient (%) ≈ (height difference (ft) / 60) / distance (NM)
  • exactly, gradient (°) = arctan(height (ft) / distance (ft))

So 1° ≈ 100 ft per NM and 1 % ≈ 60 ft per NM. A 3° glide path is about 300 ft/NM (exactly 318 ft/NM) and about 5.2 %. Per cent and degrees are not the same: 10 % ≈ 5.7°. 01.05.06.01

The rate of descent on a glide path follows: ROD (ft/min) = glide-path angle (°) × GS (NM/min) × 100, or ROD (ft/min) = gradient (%) × GS (kt). For a 3° path, ROD ≈ GS × 5. A tailwind on final raises the GS and so the ROD needed to stay on the same path. 01.05.06.02

Worked example · ILS. GS 140 kt on a 3° ILS: ROD ≈ 140 × 5 = 700 ft/min.

In general, vertical speed (ft/min) = GS (kt) × gradient (ft/NM) / 60, and gradient (ft/NM) = VS × 60 / GS. Climb gradients in SIDs are over the ground, so a tailwind needs a higher rate of climb. The standard PANS-OPS climb gradient of 3.3 % is about 200 ft/NM. 01.05.06.03

Worked example · climb rate. A climb gradient of 400 ft/NM at GS 180 kt needs VS = 180 × 400 / 60 = 1200 ft/min.

Key numbers · gradients

Relationship Value
1° ≈ 100 ft/NM
1 % ≈ 60 ft/NM
3° glide path ≈ 300 ft/NM (318) ≈ 5.2 %
ROD on 3° ≈ GS × 5
3.3 % climb ≈ 200 ft/NM
3° descent distance ≈ 3 NM per 1000 ft

Before starting a descent, the aircraft's position must be known accurately, because terrain clearance in the descent depends on where the aircraft actually is. Errors are largest after long legs without fixes, or with unreliable aids. Never start a descent below the minimum safe or en-route altitude on dead reckoning alone; in mountains, cross-check two independent sources such as DME and GNSS first. 01.05.06.04

2.10 Dead reckoning

A dead reckoning (DR) position is worked out from the last fix using heading, TAS and the forecast or last known wind over the time elapsed, or simply track and GS. It is the best estimate of position when no fix is available, and it tells you when landmarks or radio aids should appear. Its accuracy decays with time as wind errors build up. An air position uses heading and TAS only, with no wind; a DR position includes the wind. 01.07.01.01

A fix is a position found from external references: a visual pinpoint, radio aids or GNSS. Comparing the fix with the DR position shows the error in the assumed wind: the line from the DR position to the fix, divided by the time since the last fix, is the wind error vector. Use it to correct heading and GS for the rest of the flight. Repeated errors in the same direction point to a steady wind error rather than poor flying. 01.07.01.02

The speed factor (SF) is the speed divided by 60: the distance covered in one minute. TAS 120 kt is SF 2, 180 kt is SF 3, GS 420 kt is SF 7. It makes mental DR quick: time (min) = distance / SF. Use TAS for the WCA, GS for time and distance. 01.07.01.03

From the 1 in 60 rule, for small angles WCA (°) = XWC (kt) / SF. It holds up to about 15–20°. It also sets a limit: the maximum possible drift is the full wind speed / SF, so a 30 kt wind at SF 3 can never cause more than 10° of drift. 01.07.01.04

Worked example · WCA. TAS 150 kt (SF 2.5), XWC 20 kt: WCA = 20 / 2.5 = 8°.

2.11 Climb and descent planning

The TAS and wind change through a climb or descent, so problems use averages taken at a representative level. In the climb, use the TAS at 2/3 of the cruising altitude (or 2/3 of the altitude change above the departure level), because the rate of climb falls with height and the aircraft spends more time in the upper part. A climb to FL 300 uses the TAS at FL 200. 01.08.01.01

In the descent, use the TAS at 1/2 of the descent altitude, because the rate of descent is roughly constant and the time is spread evenly through the band. A descent from FL 240 to the surface uses the TAS at FL 120; if the descent ends above sea level, take half of the band actually descended. 01.08.01.02

The wind is averaged the same way: the W/V at 2/3 of the cruising altitude for the climb, interpolating between forecast levels if necessary, 01.08.02.01 and the W/V at 1/2 of the descent altitude for the descent. Strong jet-level tailwinds can greatly lengthen the descent distance, so plan the top of descent with the mid-level wind. 01.08.02.02

Then solve the TOV with the average TAS and W/V for the true track to get the average GS, and distance covered = average GS × time in the climb or descent. It is the average GS, not the cruise GS, that places the top of climb and the top of descent. 01.08.02.03

Worked example · average GS. Climb to FL 240. At FL 160 (2/3) the TAS is 300 kt and the wind a 40 kt headwind, so the average GS = 260 kt.

Most aircraft manuals give graphs or tables of time, fuel and distance to climb and descend, entered with pressure altitude, temperature, mass and wind. The results are usually in still air, so correct the distance for wind using the average GS. Climb data are often given from sea level; for an elevated aerodrome subtract the values for the aerodrome's altitude. 01.08.03.01

Time = altitude change / average rate of climb or descent, and distance = average GS × time. On a 3° path, ROD = GS × 10 / 2 = SF × 3 × 100, and the descent distance is about the height in feet / 300 NM, roughly 3 NM per 1000 ft. So a descent from 30 000 ft needs about 90–100 NM, more with a tailwind or a speed reduction. 01.08.03.02

Worked example · descent time. Descend 9000 ft at 1500 ft/min: 6 min. At GS 240 kt that is 24 NM.

The required rate to reach an altitude at a point is the height change / time available, with time = distance / GS. Always convert distance to time with GS, never TAS, and leave room to slow down before a speed constraint. 01.08.03.03

Worked example · required ROD. 10 000 ft to lose in 40 NM at GS 300 kt: time = 40 × 60 / 300 = 8 min, so ROD = 1250 ft/min.

The distance required is GS × (height change / rate). A tailwind raises the GS and so the distance, so start down earlier. 01.08.03.04

Worked example · descent distance. GS 270 kt (SF 4.5), 12 000 ft to lose at 1500 ft/min: 8 min, so 36 NM.

And the rate from distance, speed and height is rate (ft/min) = height × GS / (distance × 60), which is the same as gradient (ft/NM) × GS / 60. 01.08.03.05

Worked example · rate. 6000 ft in 20 NM at 180 kt: 6000 × 180 / (20 × 60) = 900 ft/min.

Check yourself

  1. How many NM is 1' of longitude at 60° N? About 0.5 NM, cos 60°.
  2. You must cover 300 NM over the ground at TAS 240 kt with a 40 kt tailwind. How many NAM is that? GS 280 kt, so NAM = 300 × 240 / 280 ≈ 257 NAM.
  3. Climbing at a constant CAS of 280 kt, what happens to TAS and Mach? Both rise; Mach rises faster because the speed of sound falls with temperature.
  4. What is the TAS at M 0.78 in ISA at FL 350 (−54.3 °C)? T = 218.9 K, LSS ≈ 576 kt, TAS ≈ 450 kt.
  5. TAS 120 kt and a crosswind of 18 kt. What WCA? SF 2, so 9°.
  6. On a 3° approach at GS 160 kt, what rate of descent? About 800 ft/min.
  7. From FL 330 to an airfield at sea level, roughly how far out should a 3° descent begin? About 3 NM per 1000 ft: about 100 NM in still air, more with a tailwind.
  8. Which level gives the average TAS and wind for a climb to FL 270, and for a descent from FL 270 to sea level? FL 180 for the climb; FL 135 for the descent.

chapters.label: Chapter 3
chapters.title: Visual Navigation

sections.title: 3.2 Low level, poor visibility and night

chapters.html:
Visual navigation is dead reckoning checked against the ground. The pilot flies an accurate heading and keeps time, and map reading confirms or corrects the result. This chapter covers what makes a good landmark, how the view changes at low level and at night, how terrain is shown on a chart, and what to do when a checkpoint fails to appear or you are no longer sure where you are.

3.1 What makes a good landmark

A ground feature is useful for navigation when it is unique, so that it cannot be confused with a similar one nearby; large or prominent; in contrast with its surroundings; and shown accurately on the chart. Line features such as coastlines, large rivers, motorways and railways make good collecting features, because you cannot miss crossing them. Point features such as towns with a distinctive shape, lakes, dams, masts, bridges and junctions give pinpoints. A combination is best: a railway crossing a river beside a town is far more certain than the town alone. Small roads and villages change faster than charts are revised. 02.01.01.01

3.2 Low level, poor visibility and night

At low level the field of view is small, features pass quickly and are seen at a shallow angle, and terrain can hide landmarks until the last moment. Visibility is cut by haze, mist, fog, precipitation, low cloud and smoke, and by sun glare, which is worst when flying towards a low sun and makes haze look much thicker. The workload is higher too, with obstacles, airspace and terrain to watch. In poor visibility features appear late, so plan with large, linear features and keep to DR timing. 02.01.02.01

At night, unlit ground and water are invisible. Navigation relies on lit features: towns, major roads with traffic, aerodrome beacons and lighthouses, and coastlines under moonlight. Town lights can look closer than they are and distances are hard to judge. Cloud and high ground are hard to see, so the minimum safe altitude matters even more; large dark areas such as lakes, forests or the sea can be mistaken for cloud, and the other way round. Plan the route along well-lit features and radio aids. 02.01.02.02

3.3 Map reading and checkpoints

Map reading is finding the aircraft's position by matching features on the ground with features on the chart. Work from map to ground: use the DR position and the chart to predict what should appear and when, then confirm it outside. Working the other way, seeing something and searching the map for it, easily leads to a false identification. 02.02.01.01

A visual checkpoint is an easily identified ground feature on or near the route, chosen during planning to check position and timing, and marked on the chart with its planned time. For VFR flight, checkpoints every 10–15 minutes are typical. 02.02.01.02 A good checkpoint is unmistakable, visible from a distance and from the planned altitude, and does not depend on the season or the light: a river junction, a motorway interchange, a large lake, a town of characteristic shape next to a railway, a prominent peak or a headland. Avoid single small features such as a farm or a minor road, and pick a line feature just beyond each checkpoint as a backstop in case you miss it. 02.02.01.03

At each checkpoint, comparing the DR position with the actual position shows how the real wind differs from the forecast. Use the difference to revise heading (the 1 in 60 corrections of Chapter 1) and ground speed for the next leg, and to update the ETAs. A consistent drift to one side means the wind is wrong: correct the heading, not just the position. 02.02.01.04

3.4 Position lines and fixes

A position line is a line on which the aircraft is known to be at a given time: a line through a feature in a measured direction, a coastline, a railway being crossed. Two or more position lines that cross give a fix. The fix is most accurate when the lines cross at about 90°; three lines usually form a small triangle, a cocked hat, whose size shows the error. If the lines were not observed at the same time, move the earlier one along the track by the distance flown since, to make a running fix. 02.02.01.05

A single position line cannot fix the position, but it can still check progress. A line across the track, such as a railway at right angles to the route, checks the ground speed and ETA. A line along the track checks track-keeping, that is drift. 02.02.01.06

3.5 Preparing the chart

Before flight, draw the tracks; mark distance or time ticks along them (every 10 NM or every 5 minutes, say); and add headings, checkpoints, the minimum safe altitude, frequencies and airspace. In flight, hold the chart track-up, so that features left and right of the line on the chart are left and right outside, and fold it so the current leg is visible. 02.02.01.07

3.6 Visual navigation techniques

Several techniques work together. 02.02.01.08

  • Use the DR position to know where to look and when.
  • Identify a charted feature by several characteristics at once: its shape, its size and its relation to other features.
  • Allow for season and weather: snow hides roads and small lakes, dry seasons shrink rivers, haze hides low features, lakes freeze and look like fields, and flooded fields look like lakes.
  • Distance from successive bearings. When the relative bearing of a landmark doubles, say from 45° to 90° off the nose, the distance flown between the two sightings equals the distance from the landmark at the second sighting ("doubling the angle on the bow").
  • Distance from the sighting angle. Horizontal distance ≈ height / tan(depression angle). At 45° below the horizon the distance equals the height; by the 1 in 60 rule, a feature 6° below the horizon from 3000 ft is about 5 NM away.

If there is no checkpoint at a turning point, or it cannot be identified, turn on the ETA onto the next heading and confirm with the next feature, ideally a line feature as a backstop. Do not orbit searching for the turning point: that destroys the DR. 02.02.01.09

Map reading has limits. It is difficult over featureless terrain (desert, forest, sea, snowfields), over areas full of similar features (many lakes, uniform farmland), and where charts are inaccurate or out of date. Mountains hide features and add turbulence. In such areas rely on DR, timing and radio aids, and plan more fuel and more frequent radio fixes. 02.02.01.10

The standard VFR method combines everything: fly the planned heading accurately, note the time at each checkpoint, compare with the plan, correct the heading with the 1 in 60 rule, and revise ETAs and fuel. The order is clock, map, ground: look at the clock, find on the map where you should be, then find it on the ground. Accurate heading and timing make visual navigation work; map reading confirms it. 02.02.01.14

3.7 Terrain on the chart

Contour lines join points of equal elevation above MSL. Close spacing means a steep slope, wide spacing a gentle one, and closed rings are hills (or hollows, if marked). The contour interval is given in the legend. Contours show the shape of the ground; spot heights mark the highest points. 02.02.01.11

Layer tinting colours the areas between contours with a graded scale, typically green for low ground through yellow to brown for high ground, so the relief is visible at a glance. The legend gives the height band of each colour. Layer tints show terrain only; they do not show obstacles such as masts or buildings standing above it. 02.02.01.12

From the contours you can picture the ground. In a valley the contours form Vs pointing upstream, towards higher ground; on a ridge or spur the Vs point downhill. A saddle or pass lies between two closed high areas; contours that merge mark a cliff; a wide flat area inside a high contour is a plateau. 02.02.01.13

Exam trap. In a valley the V of the contours points uphill; on a spur it points downhill.

3.8 Diversion, uncertain of position, lost

A diversion starts at once: choose the new destination, estimate the track and distance by eye or with a ruler, turn onto an approximate heading straight away (over a known point if possible), then refine the heading, time and fuel, and tell ATC.

When uncertain of position, keep flying the heading, check the DR, look for a line feature and use radio aids. Think of a circle of uncertainty around the DR position, with a radius of about 10 % of the distance flown since the last fix.

When lost, tell someone early: ATC, or 121.5 MHz with a PAN call. Climb if it is safe to do so, for better radio and visual range; conserve fuel; ask for radar or VDF help; and land before the fuel or the daylight runs out. Never descend below the safe altitude to look for your position. 02.02.02.01

Check yourself

  1. Why work from map to ground rather than ground to map? Predicting what should appear from the DR position avoids identifying the wrong feature.
  2. A railway lies at right angles across your track. What does crossing it tell you? Your progress along track (GS and ETA), but not your position across track.
  3. A church is 30° off the nose at 1012 and 60° off the nose at 1018, at GS 120 kt. How far away is it at 1018? The angle doubled, so the distance equals the distance flown: 6 min at 2 NM/min, 12 NM.
  4. From 2000 ft, a mast is 10° below the horizon. Roughly how far away is it? By the 1 in 60 rule, distance ≈ height × 60 / angle = 2000 × 60 / 10 = 12 000 ft, about 2 NM.
  5. Contours form a series of Vs pointing towards lower ground. What is the feature? A spur or ridge.
  6. The planned turning point cannot be found. What do you do? Turn onto the next heading at the ETA, then confirm with the next feature or a backstop line feature.
  7. What radius of uncertainty would you assume 50 NM after the last fix? About 5 NM.

chapters.label: Chapter 4
chapters.title: Great Circles and Rhumb Lines

sections.title: 4.2 Why the great circle is shortest

chapters.html:
There are two natural ways to fly between two points on the Earth. One is the shortest route, a great circle, whose true track changes along the way. The other keeps a constant true track, a rhumb line, and is longer. This chapter explains both, why they differ, how much they differ, and how convergency and the conversion angle link the tracks of one to the other. The next chapter shows how charts draw them.

4.1 Great circles and small circles

A great circle is any circle on the Earth's surface whose plane passes through the centre of the Earth. It cuts the Earth into two equal halves. Only one great circle passes through two given points, unless they are antipodal (exactly opposite), when there are infinitely many. A small circle is any circle whose plane does not pass through the centre; every parallel of latitude except the equator is one. 03.01.01.01

The vertex is the point of highest latitude on a great circle. There the great circle runs exactly east–west (track 090° or 270°), and the latitude of the vertex equals the inclination of the great circle to the equator. Every great circle has two vertices, one in each hemisphere, 180° of longitude apart.

Examples of great circles are the equator, every meridian together with its anti-meridian, and any other circle through the centre, such as the route from London to Los Angeles or the terminator, the line between day and night. The equator is the only parallel that is a great circle. 03.01.01.04

4.2 Why the great circle is shortest

On a sphere, the shortest path between two points is the shorter arc of the great circle through them. The great circle has the largest possible radius, the Earth's own, so it curves least between the two points; any other route, a rhumb line or a small circle, bends more and is longer. Long-haul flights therefore follow great circles, adjusted for the winds, and those routes look curved on a Mercator chart. 03.01.01.03

4.3 Rhumb lines

A rhumb line (loxodrome) cuts every meridian at the same angle, so its true track is constant. Meridians and the equator are both rhumb lines and great circles. Parallels of latitude are rhumb lines with track 090° or 270°. Any other rhumb line spirals towards a pole without ever reaching it. A constant true track is easy to fly with a compass, and on a Mercator chart a rhumb line is a straight line. 03.02.01.01

Except along a meridian or the equator, the rhumb line is longer than the great circle between the same two points, because it is not an arc of a circle through the Earth's centre. The rhumb line always lies on the equatorial side of the great circle, and the great circle on the polar side. 03.02.01.02

4.4 How much longer?

The difference between great-circle and rhumb-line distances grows with latitude and with d.long. Near the equator, or over short routes, it is negligible. On long east–west routes at high latitude it is large, because the great circle bulges strongly towards the pole. 03.03.01.01

Worked example · GC and RL distances. Along 60° N for 90° of d.long, the rhumb line is the parallel: 90 × 60 × cos 60° = 2700 NM. The great circle between the same two points is about 2485 NM, some 215 NM shorter.

4.5 Convergency

Meridians converge towards the poles. A great circle that is not a meridian or the equator therefore crosses each meridian at a different angle, and its true track changes continuously along the route. In the northern hemisphere the great-circle track increases flying east and decreases flying west; in the southern hemisphere it is the opposite. 03.01.02.01

The angle between two meridians, measured where a line joining them crosses them, is the convergency, and it equals the total change of great-circle track between those meridians. For the Earth:

Earth convergency = d.long × sin (mean latitude)

At the equator the convergency is zero (the meridians are parallel there); at the poles it equals the d.long. Note that convergency uses the sine of latitude while departure uses the cosine. 03.01.02.02

The formula is a good approximation up to about 30° of d.long. 03.01.02.03

Worked example · convergency. A at 50° N 010° W, B at 60° N 020° E. d.long = 30°, mean latitude 55°. Convergency = 30 × sin 55° = 30 × 0.819 ≈ 24.6°. If the initial great-circle track at A is 040° T, the final track at B is 040 + 24.6 ≈ 065° T: northern hemisphere, eastbound, so the track increases.

4.6 The conversion angle

The conversion angle (CA) is the angle between the great circle and the rhumb line joining two points, measured at either point. It is half the convergency: 03.03.02.01

CA = ½ × d.long × sin (mean latitude)

Because the great circle lies on the polar side of the rhumb line, the rhumb-line track is the mean of the initial and final great-circle tracks. In the northern hemisphere, eastbound, initial GC track = RL track − CA and final GC track = RL track + CA; westbound the tracks decrease instead.

Radio waves travel along great circles, so a radio bearing is a great-circle bearing. To plot one on a Mercator chart, where straight lines are rhumb lines, convert it to a rhumb-line bearing by applying the conversion angle towards the equator. On a Lambert chart, where straight lines are close to great circles, radio bearings are plotted directly, allowing only for the chart convergency between meridians (Chapter 5).

Worked example · conversion angle. RL track 080° T, d.long 20° E, mean latitude 50° N. Convergency = 20 × sin 50° = 15.3°, so CA = 7.7°. Initial GC track ≈ 080 − 7.7 = 072°, final GC track ≈ 080 + 7.7 = 088°.

Exam trap. The conversion angle is half the convergency. Sketch the meridians and the curve before answering: the great circle always bows towards the pole, and that settles every sign.

Check yourself

  1. Which parallel of latitude is a great circle? Only the equator.
  2. A great circle crosses the equator at 30° to it. What is the latitude of its vertices, and what is the track there? 30° N and 30° S; 090° or 270°.
  3. In the southern hemisphere, flying east along a great circle, does the true track increase or decrease? It decreases.
  4. Find the convergency between 040° W and 010° W at a mean latitude of 45° N. 30 × 0.707 ≈ 21.2°.
  5. The initial GC track from A to B is 058° T and the final GC track 082° T. What are the rhumb-line track and the conversion angle? RL 070° T; convergency 24°, CA 12°.
  6. Is the great-circle route between two points at 55° N north or south of the rhumb line? North, on the polar side.
  7. When is the great-circle distance equal to the rhumb-line distance? Along a meridian or the equator.

chapters.label: Chapter 5
chapters.title: Charts

sections.title: 5.2 Projections and how to recognise them
5.3 Chart convergency and the constant of the cone

chapters.html:
A chart flattens a curved Earth, and no flat chart can show everything correctly at once. Each projection keeps some properties and gives up others. This chapter sets out what ICAO asks of an aeronautical chart, how chart convergency and scale work, the three projections in the exam (Mercator, Lambert conformal conic and polar stereographic), and how to measure tracks and plot radio bearings on them.

5.1 What ICAO requires

ICAO Annex 4 requires aeronautical charts to be conformal: angles and shapes are correct over small areas, and the scale at any point is the same in every direction, so bearings and tracks can be measured correctly. Where practical, a straight line should approximate a great circle. This is why the Lambert conformal conic projection is the standard for en-route charts in middle latitudes, and the polar stereographic at high latitudes. No flat chart can be both conformal and equal-area. 04.01.01.01

5.2 Projections and how to recognise them

Charts are made by projecting the graticule onto a surface that can be laid flat. 04.02.01.01

  • Azimuthal (plane). The surface is a plane touching the Earth, usually at a pole, as in the polar stereographic. Meridians are straight lines radiating from the pole; parallels are concentric circles.
  • Cylindrical. The surface is a cylinder, usually touching the equator, as in the Mercator. Meridians are parallel straight lines; parallels are straight lines too.
  • Conical. The surface is a cone touching the Earth along one parallel, or cutting it along two, as in the Lambert. Meridians are straight lines converging towards the apex; parallels are arcs of circles.

So the graticule gives the projection away: parallel meridians mean cylindrical, converging straight meridians with arcs for parallels mean conical, and radial meridians with circular parallels mean azimuthal.

5.3 Chart convergency and the constant of the cone

On a conical chart the meridians are straight lines meeting at the apex of the cone, and the angle between two of them is the chart convergency:

Chart convergency = d.long × n, where n = sin (parallel of origin)

n is the constant of the cone. The parallel of origin is where the cone touches the Earth, or, for a cone cutting the Earth along two standard parallels, approximately midway between them. The same formula covers the other two projections as limits: the polar stereographic is a cone flattened into a plane, with n = sin 90° = 1, and the Mercator is a cone opened into a cylinder, with n = 0. Because n is constant over the whole chart, chart convergency depends only on d.long, not on latitude. 04.01.02.01

Worked example · constant of the cone. Parallel of origin 48°: n = sin 48° = 0.743. Between meridians 20° apart, chart convergency = 20 × 0.743 = 14.9°.

A straight line on a chart represents a great circle exactly only where chart convergency = Earth convergency. On a Lambert chart this happens at the parallel of origin, where sin(parallel of origin) = sin(latitude); elsewhere the straight line is a very close approximation, and the true great circle is a slight curve concave towards the parallel of origin. On a polar stereographic chart, chart convergency = d.long while Earth convergency = d.long × sin latitude, so they match exactly only at the pole and closely at high latitudes. On a Mercator chart the chart convergency is zero, so straight lines are rhumb lines. 04.01.02.02

Key numbers · convergency on charts

Chart n Chart convergency Straight line is
Mercator 0 0 a rhumb line
Lambert sin parallel of origin d.long × n ≈ great circle (exact at parallel of origin)
Polar stereographic 1 d.long ≈ great circle (exact at the pole)
The Earth itself — d.long × sin mean lat —

5.4 Scale

Scale is chart length divided by Earth distance. It can be given as a representative fraction (1:500 000), as a graduated scale line, or as a statement ("1 cm = 5 km"). On Mercator and Lambert charts the latitude graduations along a meridian also work as a scale, since 1' of latitude = 1 NM. A larger scale, such as 1:250 000, shows more detail over a smaller area than a smaller scale such as 1:1 000 000. 04.01.03.01

Earth distance = chart distance × the scale denominator. Keep the units straight: 1 km = 100 000 cm. Common scales are 1:500 000 for VFR charts and 1:1 000 000 for the ICAO World Aeronautical Chart. 04.01.03.02

Worked example · scale. At 1:500 000, 12 cm on the chart = 12 × 500 000 = 6 000 000 cm = 60 km = 32.4 NM. In reverse, 100 NM at 1:1 000 000 = 185.2 km = 18.5 cm.

5.5 Direct Mercator

The direct Mercator is a cylinder touching the equator, made conformal mathematically. Its properties follow from that. 04.02.03.01

  • Meridians are parallel, equally spaced straight lines; parallels are straight lines, spaced further apart towards the poles.
  • Chart convergency is 0, which is correct only at the equator.
  • Rhumb lines are straight; great circles are curves concave to the equator, bulging towards the pole.
  • The scale is correct at the equator (or at a stated latitude) and expands with sec latitude; the poles cannot be shown.

To plot a radio bearing (a great circle) on a Mercator chart, apply the conversion angle first (Chapter 4).

Because the scale grows as sec latitude, the representative fraction changes across the chart: denominator at latitude 2 = denominator at latitude 1 × cos lat 2 / cos lat 1. A higher latitude means a larger scale and a smaller denominator. 04.02.03.02

Worked example · Mercator scale. 1:1 000 000 at the equator. At 60° N: 1 000 000 × cos 60° / cos 0° = 1:500 000.

So a given length on the chart represents less Earth distance at higher latitude: Earth distance ∝ cos latitude. Measure distances on a Mercator chart with the latitude scale at the mid-latitude of the line. 04.02.03.03

Worked example · same length, different distance. 10 cm represents 100 NM at 30° N. At 60° N it represents 100 × cos 60° / cos 30° = 57.7 NM.

5.6 Lambert conformal conic

The Lambert is a cone that cuts the Earth along two standard parallels, made conformal. 04.02.04.01

  • Meridians are straight lines converging towards the apex (near the pole); parallels are arcs of concentric circles.
  • Chart convergency = d.long × sin(parallel of origin), constant across the chart and correct at the parallel of origin, which lies roughly midway between the standard parallels.
  • A straight line ≈ a great circle, good enough for navigation.
  • The scale is correct on the standard parallels, slightly contracted between them (least at the parallel of origin), and expanded outside them.
  • Rhumb lines are curves concave to the pole.

It is the standard ICAO chart in middle latitudes, used for Jeppesen en-route charts and the ICAO 1:500 000 chart.

The scale behaves in a set pattern. It is exactly as stated on the two standard parallels; slightly smaller between them, smallest at the parallel of origin; and it increases outside them, with distance from the parallel of origin. If the standard parallels are no more than about two-thirds of the chart's latitude range apart, the scale anywhere between them differs from the stated scale by less than 1 %, so for practical navigation it is treated as constant. 04.02.04.03

The true track of a straight line on a Lambert chart changes by the chart convergency, d.long × n, which depends only on the d.long and n, not on the latitudes of the points. 04.02.04.02

Worked example · Lambert track change. n = 0.75. A straight line from 010° W, initial track 060° T, to 020° E: d.long 30°, change = 30 × 0.75 = 22.5°, so the final track is 082.5° T (northern hemisphere, eastbound: increasing).

Turned around, the same relationship finds the unknown. If the track change of a straight line and the d.long are known, n = chart convergency / d.long and the parallel of origin = arcsin n. Use the chart convergency here, not the Earth convergency. 04.02.04.05

Worked example · parallel of origin. A straight-line track changes by 18° over 24° of d.long. n = 18 / 24 = 0.75, so the parallel of origin ≈ 48.6°.

On a printed Lambert chart, measure the angle between two meridians (the chart convergency) and divide by their d.long to get n; or read the standard parallels from the legend and take the parallel of origin as about midway between them. Meridians 10° apart that meet at 7.5° give n = 0.75, a parallel of origin of about 48.6°. 04.02.04.06

And with n and the two tracks known, d.long = (final track − initial track) / n. In the northern hemisphere, an increasing track means the second point is east of the first. 04.02.04.07

Worked example · d.long from track change. n = 0.6; the straight-line track is 075° T at A and 093° T at B. Change 18°, so d.long = 18 / 0.6 = 30°, and B is east of A.

For two positions, the rhumb-line track is the average of the initial and final great-circle tracks: initial GC = RL ∓ CA and final GC = RL ± CA, with CA = ½ × d.long × sin mean latitude. In the northern hemisphere, eastbound, initial GC < RL < final GC; westbound the tracks decrease. 04.02.04.04

Worked example · tracks between two positions. Initial GC track 050° T, final GC track 070° T. RL track = 060° T, convergency 20°, CA 10°.

5.7 Polar stereographic

The polar stereographic is projected from the opposite pole onto a plane touching the Earth at a pole. 04.02.02.01

  • It is conformal; meridians are straight lines radiating from the pole and parallels are concentric circles.
  • Chart convergency = d.long (n = 1), correct at the pole and close at high latitudes.
  • A straight line ≈ a great circle, very nearly exact near the pole.
  • The scale is correct at the pole and expands away from it: at 70° it is about 3 % larger. It is used above about 70° latitude.
  • Rhumb lines are curves concave to the pole.

True direction changes very quickly near the pole, so polar charts usually carry a grid overlay for grid navigation.

Because chart convergency = d.long, the true track of a straight line changes by exactly the d.long between its ends. On a Lambert it changes by d.long × n, and on a Mercator not at all. 04.02.02.02

Worked example · polar track change. A straight line from 70° N 020° W, initial track 080° T, to a point at 030° E: d.long 50°, eastbound in the northern hemisphere, so the final track is 080 + 50 = 130° T.

5.8 Symbols, measuring and plotting

Learn to recognise the standard ICAO Annex 4 symbols: VOR (a hexagon, usually inside a compass rose), DME (a square), VOR/DME (a hexagon inside a square), VORTAC, NDB (a circle of dots), aerodromes (civil, military or joint, with or without hard runways), obstacles (single, group, lit), airspace boundaries (controlled airspace, and prohibited P, restricted R and danger D areas), reporting points (a filled triangle is compulsory, an open one on request), spot heights and maximum elevation figures. A P area is prohibited, an R area restricted under conditions, and a D area one where hazardous activity may take place. 04.03.01.01

To measure a track, align the protractor with a meridian and measure at the mid-meridian on a Lambert chart. To measure a distance, use dividers against the latitude scale near the mid-latitude, or the chart's scale line. Convert true to magnetic with the variation at mid-track. IFR en-route charts print magnetic tracks and distances along the airways; VFR charts usually require you to measure true tracks yourself. 04.03.02.01

To fix with VOR and DME: a VOR radial is a magnetic bearing from the station, so convert it to true with the variation at the station and draw it from the station. A DME range is an arc around the station; it is slant range, which matters only close to the station at height. A radial and a DME range from the same station give a rho-theta fix; two radials, or two DME ranges, also fix the position. 04.03.02.02

An NDB bearing is measured at the aircraft, so it uses the variation at the aircraft. The ADF gives a relative bearing (RB): QDM, the magnetic bearing to the station, = MH + RB, and the true bearing to the station = TH + RB. The bearing to plot from the station is that ± 180°, but it was measured at the aircraft's meridian. On a Lambert chart, apply the chart convergency between the aircraft's and the station's meridians before plotting it from the station. Convergency can be ignored only if both meridians are the same; on a Mercator chart use the conversion angle instead. 04.03.02.03

Worked example · NDB bearing. TH 040°, RB 300°. True bearing to the station = 040 + 300 = 340° T at the aircraft, so the bearing from the station is 160° T measured at the aircraft's meridian. Apply the convergency to transfer it to the station's meridian before drawing it.

Exam trap. VOR: variation at the station. NDB: variation at the aircraft. MH + RB = QDM; TH + RB = true bearing to the station.

Check yourself

  1. Why does ICAO want charts to be conformal? So that angles, and therefore bearings and tracks, are correct.
  2. What is the constant of the cone for a Lambert chart with standard parallels 37° N and 65° N? Parallel of origin about 51°, n ≈ 0.78.
  3. On a polar stereographic chart a straight line runs from 75° N 060° W to 80° N 040° E. By how much does its true track change? By the d.long, 100°.
  4. A Mercator chart has a scale of 1:2 000 000 at 30° N. What is the scale at 50° N? 2 000 000 × cos 50° / cos 30° ≈ 1:1 484 000.
  5. Where is the scale of a Lambert chart smallest? At the parallel of origin, between the standard parallels.
  6. Which variation do you use for a VOR radial, and for an NDB bearing? Station variation for the VOR; aircraft variation for the NDB.
  7. On a Lambert chart a straight line's track changes from 070° to 088° over 25° of d.long. What is n, and the parallel of origin? n = 0.72, parallel of origin ≈ 46°.
  8. On which chart is a straight line a rhumb line? The Mercator.

sections.title: 6.1 The mean solar day and local mean time
6.3 Standard time and daylight saving time

chapters.html:
Time and longitude are two ways of saying the same thing: the Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, so every 15° of longitude is an hour of time. This chapter covers local mean time and UTC, standard and daylight saving time, the International Date Line, and the times of sunrise, sunset and twilight that decide when a flight is in daylight or at night.

6.1 The mean solar day and local mean time

The apparent solar day, from one noon to the next, is not constant. It varies through the year because the Earth's orbit is elliptical and its axis tilted. The mean solar day is the average length, exactly 24 hours, based on an imaginary mean Sun moving uniformly along the equator. Local mean time (LMT) is time kept by the mean Sun at a particular meridian: it is 12:00 LMT when the mean Sun crosses that meridian. Every meridian has its own LMT, and LMT at Greenwich is, for practical purposes, UTC. The day measured against the stars, the sidereal day, is about 23 h 56 min. 05.01.01.01

6.2 Converting longitude and time

The Earth turns 360° in 24 h, so 15° = 1 h, 1° = 4 min and 15' = 1 min. This conversion is called arc to time. East of Greenwich the Sun crosses the meridian earlier, so local time is ahead of UTC:

LMT = UTC + longitude east; LMT = UTC − longitude west

The memory aid is "longitude east, Greenwich least; longitude west, Greenwich best". If the answer crosses midnight, the date changes too, so carry the day carefully. 05.01.02.01

Worked example · arc to time. 0800 UTC at 045° E: 45° = 3 h, so LMT = 0800 + 3 h = 1100. At 082° 30' W: 82° = 5 h 28 min and 30' = 2 min, so 5 h 30 min, and LMT = 0800 − 5 h 30 min = 0230.

Key numbers · arc to time

Arc Time
360° 24 h
15° 1 h
1° 4 min
15' 1 min
1' 4 s

6.3 Standard time and daylight saving time

Standard time is the legal time used throughout a country or zone. It is usually a whole number of hours (sometimes a half) from UTC, and it is set by each state, not fixed by longitude. Daylight saving time, or summer time, usually adds one hour to standard time in summer. The values for each country are listed in the AIP (GEN 2.1) and in almanacs. Mainland Spain, for example, keeps UTC + 1 in winter and UTC + 2 in summer. Flight plans, METARs and NOTAMs use UTC; local time appears mainly for opening hours, often marked "(summer)". To go between two local times, always convert to UTC first. 05.02.01.01

6.4 The International Date Line

The International Date Line runs roughly along the 180° meridian, bending around islands and countries so that each keeps a single date. Crossing it westbound, from America towards Asia, add a day; crossing it eastbound, from Asia towards America, subtract a day. UTC itself does not change at the date line; only the local date does. The simplest way to avoid date-line mistakes is to work every timing problem in UTC. 05.02.02.01

Exam trap. Westbound across the date line the date goes forward one day; eastbound it goes back.

6.5 Sunrise, sunset and twilight

Sunrise and sunset are the moments when the upper edge (limb) of the Sun is on the visible horizon. At that moment the Sun's centre is geometrically about 50' below the horizon: 16' for the Sun's semi-diameter plus 34' for atmospheric refraction, which bends the light over the horizon.

Civil twilight is the period between sunset and the moment the Sun's centre is 6° below the horizon, and likewise in the morning before sunrise. For aviation, night is commonly defined as the time from the end of evening civil twilight to the beginning of morning civil twilight. Nautical twilight (Sun 12° below) and astronomical twilight (18°) are not used for aviation night.

Almanacs tabulate these times in LMT for a given latitude and date. Convert to UTC with the longitude (arc to time), and then to standard time if needed. 05.03.01.01

Worked example · sunset in UTC. The almanac gives sunset 1842 LMT at a place at 012° W. 12° = 48 min, and the place is west, so UTC = 1842 + 48 min = 1930 UTC.

Sunrise, sunset and twilight change with three things. 05.03.01.02

  • Date. Days lengthen in spring and summer and shorten in autumn and winter.
  • Latitude. At the equator sunrise and sunset are near 0600 and 1800 LMT all year, and twilight is short because the Sun rises and sets steeply. At higher latitudes daylight varies much more through the year and twilight lasts longer, because the Sun crosses the horizon at a shallow angle; in high-latitude summer twilight can last all night.
  • Altitude. From height you see further over the horizon, so sunrise is earlier and sunset later than on the ground. After sunset on the ground, an aircraft overhead can still be in sunlight.

The length of daylight changes fastest around the equinoxes, in March and September, when the Sun's declination changes most quickly, and most slowly around the solstices in June and December, when the declination is near its limit and almost still. For a few weeks around a solstice the day length hardly changes. 05.03.01.03

Check yourself

  1. What is 1° of longitude in time, and 1' of longitude? 4 min; 4 s.
  2. It is 2200 UTC on 3 March. What is the LMT at 120° E? 0600 LMT on 4 March.
  3. It is 1530 LMT at 073° 15' W. What is UTC? 73° 15' = 4 h 53 min, so 2023 UTC.
  4. An aircraft crosses the date line flying from Tokyo to Los Angeles. What happens to the local date? It goes back one day; UTC is unaffected.
  5. Where on the Earth is twilight shortest, and why? At the equator, because the Sun rises and sets almost vertically.
  6. What depression of the Sun ends evening civil twilight? 6° below the horizon (centre of the Sun).
  7. When does the length of the day change fastest? Around the equinoxes, in March and September.
